deep.reconstruction:
There are no formulas, computations or derivations on this page. It continues a methodological and philosophical reflection that begins on the previous page ('Die Mathematik hat anderen Wissenschaften gegen-') and runs onto the next page. Paraphrase of the argument:

(1) Mathematics has one advantage over other sciences: one can say definitely whether a question has been settled ('erledigt') or not.

(2) Chess analogy: chess, unlike science, presupposes a definite goal, mating the king. The goal is arbitrary but fixed once and for all. Whether a thought or method succeeds or fails at that goal measures its quality.

(3) In physics, nature sets the problems.

(4) In mathematics the danger of fragmentation ('Zertrennen' or 'Zersplitterung') lies in arbitrariness. This follows from the nature of the subject: the same understanding sets the problems itself, solves them, and judges and values them critically by its own measure, with no external support.

(5) The remedy is to strive for great guiding viewpoints. One should impose on oneself the duty to regard and compare every single result in relation to the whole of science.

(6) Consequence: working through the existing material is better than everyone digging further in his own heap ('Mist'), which nobody cares about anyway. Anyone who writes reviews ('Referate') sees that many practise science this way, 'to nobody's joy and to their own torment'.

(7) The sentence continues on the next page: what matters is not the settling of particular questions. Those serve only as guiding motif, goal and lure. What matters is that the edifice of science rises harmoniously and in unity.

The surrounding pages give context. The previous page introduces the idea that one must at least solve the 'next superordinate question' F^2. The next page uses F^2 as a possible criterion for how important a question is. It also distinguishes a bare finiteness proof (as in Hilbert's own finiteness theorem for invariants of ternary forms) from an explicit upper bound on the number of processes. Finally it asks whether some mathematical problems cannot be settled within a prescribed small time.

So this page is the epistemological core of that passage: mathematics is a domain where 'settled or not' can be decided, a kind of early decidability optimism. Its problem-setting, however, is autonomous and so needs unifying viewpoints. It is a precursor in spirit to the 1900 Paris address (solvability of every problem, unity of mathematics) and to the later use of the chess analogy around formalism.

results.what: Claim that in mathematics one can always determine definitely whether a question is settled (early form of Hilbert's conviction about the decidability/solvability of every mathematical problem).
results.modern_name: Hilbert's solvability axiom / 'Non-ignorabimus' optimism; precursor to the Entscheidungsproblem mindset
results.usually_credited_to: David Hilbert, publicly in the Paris address (1900) and 'Naturerkennen und Logik' (1930)

results.what: Analogy between mathematics and chess: a fixed, arbitrary but once-for-all goal (checkmate) against which the quality of a method is measured.
results.modern_name: Chess analogy for formal/goal-directed mathematics (later associated with formalism debates, e.g. Weyl's and Hilbert's 1920s remarks)
results.usually_credited_to: Commonly associated with the 1920s formalism debate (Hilbert, Weyl, von Neumann); also Frege/Thomae on 'game formalism'

results.what: Methodological maxim: avoid fragmentation by seeking great unifying viewpoints and relating each result to the whole of mathematics; criticism of isolated specialist work seen through reviewing.
results.modern_name: Unity of mathematics (Hilbert's 'organic whole' theme, 1900 Paris address)
results.usually_credited_to: David Hilbert (1900 Paris lecture), also Klein

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains no mathematics, only methodological reflection. The themes (decidability of mathematical questions, unity of mathematics, danger of fragmentation) are well known as Hilbert's from the 1900 Paris address and later writings. The private, pre-1900 formulation and the early chess analogy are a pleasant biographical detail. Scholars working on Hilbert's notebooks (e.g. Rowe, Corry) have discussed such passages, so this is of modest novelty.
transcription_corrections: 'die Güte der Gedankens-' should read 'die Güte des Gedankens (der Methode)'.
'Durcharbeiten der vorhandenen Stoffes' should read 'Durcharbeiten des vorhandenen Stoffes'.
'freilich willkürli-[-chen-]' : the first word of the next line is struck out. It reads like a cancelled start ('Wi-' or 'ihr'), not the syllable '-chen'; the intended adjective is 'willkürlichen'.

'Gefahr der Zertrennens' : the image shows 'Zertrennens' (with initial Z resembling F). The intended sense is 'Zersplitterung/Zertrennung' (fragmentation); the grammatical form should be 'des Zertrennens'.
'vor der Wissenschaft' : there is a correction over the article ('der' overwritten); 'vor den Wissenschaften' is possible but less likely.
'seinen eigenen Mist weitergräbt' : the reading 'Mist' looks correct from the image (heap/dung), not a transcription error.
'[-in-] der That' : the struck word before 'der That' is a short cancelled word, probably 'ist' or 'in'.
